blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 19 (Basics of Organic Chemistry), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Define organic chemistry according to IUPAC. What is catenation? Explain how catenation and the tetravalency of carbon account for the vast number of organic compounds. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Organic chemistry (IUPAC): the study of compounds containing carbon, where carbon is bonded to itself, hydrogen or other elements, excluding some inorganic compounds (carbonates, cyanides such as KCN, CO₂, CO). More than 20 million carbon compounds are known.

Catenation: the ability of self-linkage between atoms of the same element (Latin catena = chain).
• Carbon forms long chains and rings through stable C–C covalent bonds; this self-linking has unique importance in organic chemistry.
• Carbon is tetravalent, so carbon atoms can be arranged in many different ways (straight chains, branched chains, rings). For example, four carbon atoms give four different arrangements.

Result: catenation together with tetravalency explains why organic compounds are complex, have large structures and show vast diversity. Organic compounds are also recognised by low m.p and b.p, low densities and low solubility in water.

book_ref.quote: Catenation explains why organic compounds are complex

blocks.prompt: 2 What are hydrocarbons? Describe the classification of hydrocarbons on the basis of carbon skeleton, with examples of each class. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Hydrocarbons: compounds containing carbon and hydrogen only.

On the basis of carbon skeleton they are of two types:

1. Open chain (acyclic) or aliphatic hydrocarbons: carbon atoms form an open chain ('aleiphatos', Greek for fat; fats have open chain structure).
• Saturated: alkanes.
• Unsaturated: alkenes and alkynes.

2. Closed chain or cyclic hydrocarbons: carbon atoms form rings.
• Alicyclic hydrocarbons: cyclic, saturated or unsaturated, which behave like aliphatic hydrocarbons, e.g. cycloalkanes, cycloalkenes.
• Aromatic hydrocarbons: having a benzene ring or resembling structures, e.g. benzene, naphthalene, diphenyl methane.

book_ref.quote: On the basis of carbon skeleton, hydrocarbons are broadly classified into two types

blocks.prompt: 3 Define functional group. Explain with examples how functional groups affect the physical properties of organic compounds. Why do alkanes have no functional group? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Functional group: an atom or group of atoms, or the presence of a double or triple bond, which determines the characteristic properties of an organic compound.

Effect on properties: both physical and chemical properties depend strongly on the functional group.
• Physical state: methanol and ethanol are liquids, while methane and ethane are gases.
• m.p and b.p: alcohols have higher m.p and b.p than the corresponding alkanes, because the hydroxyl group (–OH) forms hydrogen bonds; alkanes cannot.
• Solubility: lower alcohols, carboxylic acids, glucose and sucrose dissolve in polar solvents like water because of their polar functional groups.

The type of organic compound is dictated by (i) polarity of the bond and (ii) bond order (number of bonds) in the functional group.

Alkanes and cycloalkanes have no functional group, as they possess no charges or polarity and no double or triple bonds.

book_ref.quote: Both physical and chemical properties of organic compounds are highly affected

blocks.prompt: 4 Describe the components of a systematic (IUPAC) name of an organic compound. Split 3-methylbut-2-en-1-ol into its components. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The IUPAC name is based on the parent hydrocarbon and has three components:

(i) Stem or root: the longest continuous carbon chain including the carbon bearing the functional group; the lowest possible number is given to that carbon. For a ring, the name starts with 'cyclo'.

(ii) Suffix:
• Primary suffix (suffix of stem): shows whether the parent chain is saturated or unsaturated (an, en).
• Secondary suffix (suffix of the key functional group): gives the family name (ol, al, one ...).

(iii) Prefix: the name of the side chain (alkyl group) or substituent (halo, nitro ...) with the number of the carbon to which it is attached. If the prefix is absent, the name is root + suffix.

3-methylbut-2-en-1-ol: prefix 3-methyl; stem but (4 C); primary suffix 2-en (C=C at carbon 2); secondary suffix 1-ol (OH on carbon 1).

book_ref.quote: along with number of carbon atom to which it is attached

blocks.prompt: 5 Give the general formula, functional group and IUPAC class name of alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters and ethers, with one named example of each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: The oxygen-containing classes:

book_ref.quote: Each name consists of the components listed below

blocks.prompt: 6 Describe the nomenclature of amines (primary, secondary, tertiary), alkyl cyanides and nitroalkanes, giving one correctly named example of each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Amines (CₙH₂ₙ₊₁NH₂), three types:
• Primary (–C–NH₂): alkanamine, e.g. CH₃–CH₂–NH₂ ethanamine; CH₃–CH(NH₂)–CH₃ propan-2-amine.
• Secondary (–C–NH–R): N-alkylalkanamine; nitrogen carries one H, e.g. CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–NH–CH₃ N-methylpropan-1-amine.
• Tertiary (–C–N(R)–R): N,N-dialkylalkanamine when the two groups on N are the same, e.g. CH₃CH₂CH₂–N(CH₃)–CH₃ N,N-dimethylpropan-1-amine; N-alkyl-N-alkylalkanamine when they differ, e.g. CH₃CH₂CH₂–N(CH₃)–CH₂CH₃ N-ethyl-N-methylpropan-1-amine.

2. Alkyl cyanides (CₙH₂ₙ₋₁N, –C≡N): alkanenitrile (CN carbon counted), e.g. CH₃–CN ethanenitrile; CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CN 2-methylpropanenitrile.

3. Nitroalkanes (CₙH₂ₙ₊₁NO₂, –C–NO₂): nitroalkane, e.g. CH₃–NO₂ nitromethane; CH₃–CH(NO₂)–CH₃ 2-nitropropane.

book_ref.quote: There are three types of amines

blocks.prompt: 7 Give the functional group, IUPAC class name and two named examples each of alkyl halides, acid amides, acid halides and acid anhydrides. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Classes and their names:

book_ref.quote: The IUPAC name is alkanamide

rows: CH₃COCl ethanoyl chloride; CH₃CH₂COCl propanoyl chloride
(CH₃CO)₂O ethanoic anhydride; CH₃CO–O–COCH₂CH₃ ethanoic propanoic anhydride

blocks.prompt: 8 Describe the molecular, empirical and structural formulae of organic compounds. Explain the three types of structural formula, using ethanol as the example. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Molecular formula: shows the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule, e.g. butane C₄H₁₀, ethanol C₂H₆O. It gives no information about the sequence of atoms or the functional group, so ethanol and methoxymethane share C₂H₆O.

2. Empirical formula: the smallest whole number ratio of atoms, e.g. butane C₂H₅, ethanoic acid CH₂O.

3. Structural formula: shows the number of each kind of atom and the sequence in which they are joined. Types:
(a) Displayed (graphical) formula: shows all bonds between atoms, the type of bonds and positions of functional groups. For ethanol every C–H, C–C, C–O and O–H bond is drawn.
(b) Condensed (linear) formula: a one-line form; single bonds omitted, branches and functional groups in brackets. Ethanol: CH₃CH₂OH.
(c) Skeletal (bond-line) formula: C and H symbols and C–H bonds removed; C–C bonds are lines meeting at an angle, each carbon making four bonds; functional groups shown. Ethanol: a short line with OH at one end.

book_ref.quote: There are different types of structural formulae.

blocks.prompt: 9 Deduce the molecular and empirical formulae of the compounds represented by these skeletal formulae: (i) a zig-zag of five single lines with no atom symbols; (ii) a zig-zag of four lines in which the first line is a double line; (iii) two single lines meeting at a joint which carries a double line to O. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Count one C at each joint and each line end (unless another atom is written), then add H to give every carbon four bonds; divide by the common factor for the empirical formula.

book_ref.quote: Count the C atoms represented and the heteroatoms shown in the skeleton

steps: (i) Five lines join 6 points, so 6 C. End carbons need 3 H each, the 4 middle carbons 2 H each: H = 2 × 3 + 4 × 2 = 14. Molecular formula C₆H₁₄; 6 : 14 = 3 : 7, empirical formula C₃H₇.
(ii) Four lines join 5 points, so 5 C. C-1 (=CH₂) has 2 H, C-2 (=CH–) 1 H, C-3 and C-4 2 H each, C-5 3 H: H = 2 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 10. Molecular formula C₅H₁₀; 5 : 10 = 1 : 2, empirical formula CH₂.

(iii) Two lines give 3 C; the middle carbon is joined to O by a double bond and has no H; each end carbon has 3 H: H = 6. Molecular formula C₃H₆O (propanone); 3 : 6 : 1 cannot be simplified, so empirical formula C₃H₆O.
blocks.final_answer: (i) C₆H₁₄, empirical C₃H₇; (ii) C₅H₁₀, empirical CH₂; (iii) C₃H₆O, empirical C₃H₆O

blocks.prompt: 10 Using the general formulae of the classes, find the molecular and empirical formulae of (i) an alcohol with 3 carbon atoms (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂O), (ii) a carboxylic acid with 4 carbon atoms (CₙH₂ₙO₂), (iii) an alkyl cyanide with 3 carbon atoms (CₙH₂ₙ₋₁N), (iv) an acid amide with 3 carbon atoms (CₙH₂ₙ₋₁ONH₂). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Put the value of n in the general formula to get the molecular formula, then divide all subscripts by their highest common factor to get the empirical formula.

book_ref.quote: The formula which represents the smallest whole number ratio of atoms of each element

steps: (i) n = 3: H = 2(3) + 2 = 8, so C₃H₈O. Ratio 3 : 8 : 1 has no common factor, empirical formula C₃H₈O.
(ii) n = 4: H = 2(4) = 8, O = 2, so C₄H₈O₂. Common factor 2, empirical formula C₂H₄O.
(iii) n = 3: H = 2(3) – 1 = 5, so C₃H₅N. Ratio 3 : 5 : 1, empirical formula C₃H₅N.
(iv) n = 3: C₃H₅O·NH₂ = C₃H₇NO. Ratio 3 : 7 : 1 : 1, empirical formula C₃H₇NO.
blocks.final_answer: (i) C₃H₈O / C₃H₈O; (ii) C₄H₈O₂ / C₂H₄O; (iii) C₃H₅N / C₃H₅N; (iv) C₃H₇NO / C₃H₇NO

blocks.prompt: 11 Describe the formation of free radicals, carbocations and carbanions as reactive intermediates when covalent bonds break. Give one example of each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Free radicals (homolysis): when a nonpolar bond breaks, the two shared electrons are distributed equally, each atom keeping one unpaired electron (shown by a dot).
Cl–Cl → Cl• + Cl•;  H₃C–H → H₃C• + H•
Free radicals are reaction intermediates and highly reactive because their unpaired electrons tend to be paired.

2. Carbocations (heterolysis of a polar bond): one atom keeps both electrons and becomes negative; the other becomes positive. When carbon is bonded to an atom more electronegative than carbon (e.g. O, N, halogens), carbon loses the pair and a carbocation forms.
(CH₃)₃C–Cl → (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Cl⁻

3. Carbanions: formed when carbon is bonded to a metal less electronegative than carbon (e.g. Li, Mg, Cd); carbon keeps the pair and becomes negative, e.g. CH₃⁻ from CH₃–Li.

book_ref.quote: Carbocation is formed when carbon is bonded to a heteroatom whose electronegativity is more than carbon

blocks.prompt: 12 What are reagent and substrate? Describe the three types of reagents with examples, and explain how polar molecules can be electrophilic or nucleophilic. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
A reaction between two reactants is regarded as the attack of one species on the other: the attacking species is the reagent; the species being attacked is the substrate.

Types of reagents:
(i) Free radicals: atoms or groups with unpaired electrons, e.g. Cl•, H•, •CH₃, CH₃COO•.
(ii) Electrophiles (electron lovers): accept a pair of electrons to form a new bond; positive ions (including carbocations) or neutral molecules, e.g. CH₃⁺, H⁺, Br⁺, NO₂⁺, SO₃, BF₃.
(iii) Nucleophiles (nucleus lovers): donate a pair of electrons to form a new bond; negative ions (including carbanions) or neutral molecules, e.g. CH₃⁻, Br⁻, OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃, H₂O, ROH.

Polar molecules: the terms do not apply only to ions. Many organic molecules carry partial charges:
• CH₃(δ+)–OH(δ–): carbon electrophilic, OH nucleophilic.
• CH₃(δ–)–Li(δ+): carbon nucleophilic, Li electrophilic.

book_ref.quote: A chemical reaction between two reactants may be regarded as the attack of one species on the other

blocks.prompt: 13 Describe substitution, addition and elimination reactions with one equation each. Why is elimination regarded as the reverse of addition? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Substitution: an atom or group in one molecule is replaced by another atom or group; two products may form.
CH₃–CH₂–Br + KOH(aq) →(H₂O) CH₃–CH₂–OH + KBr  (bromoethane → ethanol)

2. Addition: two reactants react to give a single product.
CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ →(Ni, 200–300 °C) CH₃–CH₃  (ethene → ethane)
CH₃–CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃–CHBr–CH₃  (main product 2-bromopropane, Markovnikov's rule)

3. Elimination: atoms or groups are removed from two adjacent atoms of the substrate to form a multiple bond.
CH₃–CH₂–Br + KOH →(alcohol) CH₂=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O  (bromoethane → ethene)

Addition converts a multiple bond into single bonds by adding atoms; elimination removes atoms and creates the multiple bond, so it is regarded as the reverse of addition.

book_ref.quote: Two products may be formed. For example

blocks.prompt: 14 Explain hydrolysis, condensation, oxidation and reduction reactions of organic compounds, giving one equation for each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Hydrolysis: a compound breaks into two on reaction with water, often helped by H⁺ or OH⁻ as catalyst.
CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + H₂O →(H⁺) CH₃COOH + CH₃CH₂OH  (ethyl ethanoate → ethanoic acid + ethanol)

2. Condensation: two molecules combine to form a bigger molecule, with or without loss of a small molecule (H₂O, NH₃, HCl).
CH₃COCH₃ + H₂N–OH → CH₃C(CH₃)=N–OH + H₂O  (propanone + hydroxylamine → propanone oxime)

3. Oxidation: loss of electrons; for a molecule, gain of oxygen, loss of hydrogen, increase in C–O bonds or in the oxidation state of carbon.
CH₃–CH=CH₂ →(O₃; Zn/H₂O) CH₃CHO + HCHO  (propene → ethanal + methanal)

4. Reduction: gain of electrons, loss of oxygen, gain of hydrogen, decrease in C–O bonds or in the oxidation state of carbon.
CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ →(Ni) CH₃–CH₃  (ethene → ethane)

book_ref.quote: Moreover, if a molecule gains oxygen or loses hydrogen

blocks.prompt: 15 What is a reaction mechanism? Describe the free radical mechanism, taking the chlorination of methane in diffused sunlight as the example. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Mechanism: the pathway adopted by a reaction showing the breaking and making of bonds in the substrate leading to the product. Depending on the reagents there are two main types: free radical and ionic (polar).

Free radical mechanism: involves homolysis, producing free radicals which attack the substrate molecule.
Overall: CH₄ + 4Cl₂ →(diffused sunlight) CCl₄ + 4HCl

Steps: Initiation → Propagation → Termination
• Initiation: initial free radicals are produced by homolysis, e.g. Cl–Cl → 2Cl•.
• Propagation: these radicals generate more radicals, so the reaction continues as a chain until the product CCl₄ forms.
• Termination: the reaction stops when free radicals of the same or different types combine.

book_ref.quote: This reaction proceeds through the free radical mechanim

blocks.prompt: 16 Describe the ionic (polar) mechanism. Explain nucleophilic substitution, nucleophilic addition, electrophilic addition and elimination, with one example each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The ionic or polar mechanism involves heterolysis, producing electrophiles and nucleophiles which attack polar substrate molecules. Types:

(i) Nucleophilic substitution: a nucleophile attacks a saturated electrophilic carbon and replaces another nucleophile, the leaving group.
OH⁻ + CH₃–Br → [transition state] → CH₃–OH + Br⁻

(ii) Nucleophilic addition: a nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbon of a carbonyl compound to give an addition product.
Cyanide ion adds to ethanal, CH₃CHO, giving 2-hydroxypropanenitrile.

(iii) Electrophilic addition: an electrophile attacks an electron-rich (nucleophilic) position such as a C=C or C≡C bond.
CH₂=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃–CH₂Br (bromoethane)

(iv) Elimination: two atoms or groups are removed from two adjacent carbon atoms, forming a double or triple bond.
OH⁻ + CH₃–CH₂Br → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O + Br⁻ (the carbon bonded to Br is δ+, Br being more electronegative).

book_ref.quote: The polar mechanism is further divided into the following types

blocks.prompt: 17 Define isomerism. Describe the classification of isomers into structural isomers and stereoisomers, and the further division of stereoisomers. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Isomers: two or more compounds having the same molecular formula but different arrangement of atoms and different properties; the phenomenon is isomerism. E.g. ethanol and methoxymethane (C₂H₆O).

Isomerism stems from two features:
1. Structural (constitutional) isomerism: the same groups or atoms are connected at different places in the molecules (studied in Chemistry 11).
2. Stereoisomerism: the substituents have different spatial arrangement, i.e. different configuration.

Stereoisomers are further divided into:
(a) Optical isomers: identical physical and chemical properties except their ability to rotate plane polarised light; e.g. (+) and (–) lactic acid.
(b) Cis-trans isomers: differ in spatial arrangement due to restricted rotation about a double bond in open chain compounds; e.g. cis- and trans-but-2-ene.

book_ref.quote: The isomerism of organic compounds stems from the two distinct features

blocks.prompt: 18 What is plane polarised light? Describe how a polarimeter is used to find whether a compound is optically active, and explain the terms dextrorotatory and levorotatory. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Plane polarised light (PPL): monochromatic light of a single wavelength which moves only in one plane.

Polarimeter: used to identify and measure quantitatively the optical activity of a compound using PPL (Figure 19.4).
• A solution of the compound under investigation is placed in the path of PPL.
• If the compound rotates the plane of PPL, it is optically active; if not, it is optically inactive.
• The property of rotating the plane of polarisation is called optical activity.

Direction of rotation:
• Dextrorotatory (+): rotates the plane of PPL to the right (clockwise).
• Levorotatory (–): rotates the plane to the left (anticlockwise).
E.g. (+) lactic acid and (–) lactic acid.

book_ref.quote: A solution of the compound under investigation is placed before PPL

blocks.prompt: 19 Explain chirality and the chiral carbon atom. How is optical activity related to the structure of a compound? Use the analogy of hands. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Basic requirement: a compound is optically active only if it is non-superimposable on its mirror image. Such molecules are asymmetric or chiral.

Hands analogy (Figure 19.5): our right and left hands are mirror images but cannot be superimposed. 'Chiral' comes from the Greek 'cheir' (hand), so chirality is also called handedness.

Achiral: molecules superimposable on their mirror images are achiral and optically inactive.

Chiral carbon: a carbon atom bearing four different atoms or groups. A non-symmetric molecule that rotates PPL is a chiral (asymmetric) molecule.
• One chiral carbon: the molecule is always asymmetric and optically active, e.g. lactic acid, whose chiral carbon carries CH₃, H, OH and COOH.
• More than one chiral carbon: the molecule may or may not be asymmetric and optically active (e.g. meso tartaric acid is inactive).

book_ref.quote: It can be understood by considering an analogy of our right and left hands

blocks.prompt: 20 What are enantiomers? Explain with lactic acid. What is a racemic mixture and why is it optically inactive? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Enantiomers ('enantio' = opposite): two stereoisomers which are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.

Lactic acid: has one chiral carbon (marked *) bonded to four different groups, CH₃, H, OH and COOH. Its three dimensional structure gives two non-superimposable mirror images: (+) lactic acid and (–) lactic acid.

Properties: enantiomers have identical physical and chemical properties but rotate PPL in opposite directions to the same extent; one is dextrorotatory (+), the other levorotatory (–).

Racemic mixture: a mixture of 50% dextrorotatory and 50% levorotatory enantiomers. The equal and opposite rotations cancel, so it is optically inactive. It is symbolised by (±) before the name. Thus lactic acid exists as (+), (–) and the inactive racemic mixture (±).

book_ref.quote: Its three dimensional structure shows that it has two stereoisomers

blocks.prompt: 21 What are meso isomers? Explain internal compensation with tartaric acid as the example. State the rule for the maximum number of optical isomers and when it does not hold. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Meso isomers: stereoisomers which contain at least two similar chiral carbon atoms and also possess a plane of symmetry; they are optically inactive.

Internal compensation: the plane of symmetry divides the molecule into two equal halves, one half being the mirror image of the other. The two halves rotate PPL in opposite directions, so the rotation of one half is cancelled (compensated) by the other half within the same molecule. Tartaric acid is the classic example of this (meso tartaric acid).

Rule: maximum number of optical isomers = 2ⁿ, where n is the number of chiral carbon atoms. E.g. n = 1 gives 2, n = 2 gives 4, n = 3 gives 8.

Exception: the number is reduced if there are two or more similar chiral carbon atoms, because a meso form appears, as in tartaric acid.

book_ref.quote: Maximum number of optical isomers of an optically active compound is given by the formula

blocks.prompt: 22 Compare rotation about the C–C single bond in butane with rotation about the C=C double bond in but-2-ene. Explain why rotation about the double bond is restricted. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Butane: when the C-2–C-3 single bond rotates, the methyl groups rotate too and form I changes into form II and back (free rotation). Forms I and II are conformational isomers; being interconvertible, they cannot be separated at room temperature.

But-2-ene, CH₃–CH=CH–CH₃: C-2 and C-3 are sp² hybridized.
• The C=C bond has a σ bond (linear overlap of sp² hybrid orbitals) and a π bond (parallel, sideways overlap of p orbitals).
• The π bond locks the molecule in one position; C-2, C-3 and all groups attached to them lie in one plane with fixed positions.
• Free rotation would need the π bond to be broken first, requiring 263 kJ/mol, which is not possible at room temperature.

So rotation about C=C is restricted, and this restriction is responsible for cis-trans isomerism (Figure 19.6): the two forms of but-2-ene cannot interconvert.

book_ref.quote: First of all we consider free rotation about C-C single bond in butane

blocks.prompt: 23 State the necessary and sufficient condition for an open chain compound to show cis-trans isomerism. Which of these show it: CH₃–CH=CH–CH₃, H₂C=CH–CH₂–CH₃, (H₃C)₂C=C(CH₃)₂? How do cis and trans isomers differ in properties? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Condition: the compound must have a double bond, and two different groups must be attached to each of the doubly bonded carbon atoms. Cis-trans isomerism is not possible if one unsaturated carbon is bonded to two identical groups.

Cis isomer: two similar groups on the same side of the double bond. Trans isomer: two similar groups on opposite sides.

Test:
• CH₃–CH=CH–CH₃ (but-2-ene): each double-bond carbon carries H and CH₃, so it shows cis-trans isomerism (cis- and trans-but-2-ene).
• H₂C=CH–CH₂–CH₃ (but-1-ene): C-1 carries two H atoms, so no cis-trans isomerism.
• (H₃C)₂C=C(CH₃)₂ (2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene): each carbon carries two CH₃ groups, so no cis-trans isomerism.

Properties: cis and trans isomers have different physical and chemical properties. The trans isomer is more stable than the cis isomer and differs in reactivity; they differ in m.p, b.p, dipole moment, density and heat of vapourisation.

book_ref.quote: for an open chain compound the necessary and sufficient condition to show cis-trans isomerism

blocks.prompt: 24 Explain the importance of stereochemistry in drug development, describing the case of thalidomide. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Importance: in the synthesis of pharmaceutical products, chirality is critical for safety and efficacy. Biological systems are built from chiral building blocks, and drug receptors act as highly specific 'chiral locks', so the two enantiomers of a chiral drug often show very different potencies and profiles.

Thalidomide (Figure 19.7):
• A tranquilliser, originally distributed as a racemic mixture; it seemed a very successful, non-toxic sedative.
• In the early 1960s, women prescribed it for nausea (morning sickness) in early pregnancy gave birth to badly deformed babies; the drug was immediately withdrawn.
• Research showed the (+) isomer was an effective and safe tranquilliser, while the (–) isomer damaged the fetus.
• Even the pure (+) isomer racemises rapidly in the blood stream (over 50% within 10 minutes), so separating the isomers does not remove the danger.
• It has since been marketed again only under strict controls (USA: 1998 for a complication of leprosy, 2006 for multiple myeloma) with a pregnancy-prevention programme; chirally stable analogues are being investigated as anti-inflammatory drugs.

book_ref.quote: Consequently, the two enantiomers of a chiral drug often exhibit
